headline: Highest risk is data leakage: Chatwoot handles customer data and broad egress, while Argo Workflows can move artifacts/parameters through APIs, creating a plausible cross-system exposure path.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared channel is documented, so direct prompt injection is not established. However, Argo Workflows can pass artifacts/parameters and Chatwoot can ingest messages via integrations, so a manual or file-based bridge could let attacker-controlled content influence the other agent. The pathway is plausible but not default.
conditions: IF an operator copies Chatwoot content into Argo artifacts or parameters
IF a Chatwoot integration forwards untrusted text into a workflow input
mitigations: Restrict copy-paste bridges between systems
Label workflow inputs as untrusted
Add a quick human review step before execution
Use separate workspaces for support text and workflow specs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, interaction history, orders, and messages, while Argo Workflows handles artifacts and parameters and has allowlisted egress. A shared workspace or exported artifact could leak sensitive support data into workflow outputs or external calls. The pairwise path is inferred from documented surfaces, so uncertainty remains but the risk is real.
conditions: IF customer records or messages are placed into Argo artifacts or parameters
IF either system writes shared files that the other uploads or exports
mitigations: Keep customer data out of workflow artifacts
Use separate storage buckets or directories
Redact messages before passing them to workflows
Disable unnecessary outbound integrations
Review egress allowlists for sensitive jobs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Argo Workflows can call REST and gRPC APIs, and Chatwoot exposes multiple integrations and broad network egress. Even without explicit filesystem write claims, both can act on shared mutable external resources through APIs, creating overlap and possible race conditions. Because write-locking is undocumented, uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents update the same ticketing, messaging, or webhook-backed resource
IF no external locking or idempotency keys are used
mitigations: Assign one system as the source of truth
Add idempotency keys to shared API writes
Serialize updates through a single queue
Turn on optimistic concurrency checks where available

D_cascading_error.rationale: Argo can produce artifacts and parameters that Chatwoot integrations may consume, and Chatwoot can then act on those inputs through support workflows. If Chatwoot treats workflow output as authoritative, a bad upstream artifact can cascade into incorrect customer responses or routing. The interaction is inferred rather than directly documented, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF Chatwoot automation consumes Argo-generated text without verification
IF workflow outputs are used to draft or route customer replies
mitigations: Require human review before sending replies
Validate workflow outputs against schemas
Add provenance labels to generated artifacts
Reject unsupported or low-confidence fields

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot clearly processes customer data and interaction history, while Argo Workflows processes artifacts and parameters that may contain regulated content. The profiles do not document residency, retention, or certification alignment, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because the data classes are sensitive and the policies are unknown, medium is warranted.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is routed through Argo artifacts or logs
IF retention or residency policies differ between the two systems
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in workflow logs
Document retention settings for both systems
Separate EU and non-EU workloads
Review vendor compliance docs before deployment
